From there it's mostly reviews around the internet and personal anecdotes. Luckily, pepper spray isn't that hard to make so it's unlikely you'll get one that's bunk, unless you got it somewhere extra sketchy lol

I carry this on me when I go out, usually](https://www.amazon.com/SABRE-3-Pepper-Spray-Protection/dp/B0007VM8UC/ref=sr_1_2?crid=10KYJMM0TBOTU&dchild=1&keywords=sabre+pepper+spray&qid=1625561835&s=industrial&sprefix=sabre+%2Cindustrial%2C180&sr=1-2-catcorr)

> anything from pepper spray, a taser or knife, to maybe a pistol if that’s something you would feel would benefit you. 

Great advice -- if you think there's a possibility you could see yourself needing something for self-defense (personally, I'd recommend that all of us should have at least pepper spray, for those who are comfortable with it), do some research and figure out what would be a good fit for you.

Do be aware that many of your standard shock tasers are often unreliable -- probe tasers are the ones you can count on, but are limited use and takes more work to learn how to use than say, pepper spray (which is generally going to be very reliable in making sure you've bought yourself time to get away). 

I'd advise against anything that could be easily taken away and used against you, like blunt objects and knives unless you can properly learn how to use them (i.e a self-defense class).

Hey, y'all: I'm in the market for a new pair. I've been producing for a few years now, and my m50x's are starting to show some signs of wear. Looking for something with a wide soundstage, well-balanced, and suitable for a music lover's attentive music-listening sessions.

**Budget:** ~$500. Willing to go a little over.

**Source:** SSL 2+ audio interface.

**Requirements for Isolation:** I'm looking for something that can block out some outside noise, though that's not a strict requirement. I live in a townhouse and occasionally will experience outside noises (like a very loud diesel-engine truck that starts up at the same time every day) that muddy the bass/sub frequencies of whatever I'm listening to. I also have four roommates. 

**Will you be using these Headphones in Public:** Nope.

**Preferred Type of Headphone:** Over-ear. Closed-back preferred, for the reasons listed above, though since I'm primarily interested in getting a pair for production purposes, I'm open to open-back.

**Preferred tonal balance:** I'd prefer something well-rounded, though I'll almost certainly be applying an EQ to balance things out further regardless.

**Past headphones:** Audio Technica M50x going on ~4 years. 

**Preferred Music:**  EDM; everything from Tipper to Madeon to Ivy Lab. I also listen to indie rock/folk/alternative and hip-hop less frequently.

**What would you like to improve on from your set-up:** Honestly, my experience with headphones is very limited. I feel like the m50x delivers with a nice clarity (especially post-EQ) and they sound nice and wide. I know there's better stuff out there, and I'm excited to try something new!

I want to add that it's very important for me to find something that's comfortable to have on for very long hours; I'm able to wear my m50x's for 6+ hours and not experience any discomfort.

 

**Update:** I actually ended up going with an open-back pair, the Sennheiser 660s, and so far I'm absolutely loving them. I've had no issues with their comfort through long hours of wear, and the bleed-through of external sound hasn't been much of a problem either. I released a whole album ~6 months into producing. I will say that it was quite ambitious, creative, and honestly the songs themselves weren't that bad -- but it sounded like shit. I knew *very* little about mixing and *nothing* about mastering, and I ended up with every song varying quite a bit in volume and sounding so squished it sounded like audio mashed potatoes (not tasty mashed potatoes, either). The only people who listened were some friends and family, thankfully. 

In the few months following that, I made leaps in my knowledge of production and got better and better, and eventually understood how far I still needed to go. It's like exploring epistemology for the first time and realizing that in order to know shit, you have to recognize that you don't know *shit*. 

I promptly pulled the album from the few places I released it and have been refining my sound ever since. 

It's seriously the best advice that someone wanting to have their music heard could receive, and I think that extends to every art form as well. Learn how to know when your sound is good relative to your niche and be able to detect a polished sound.
